newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD-US supply, G7 meeting overhang markets.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-US supply, G7 meeting overhang markets.

text.p: International investors will focus more on supply and less on data in the coming week as the U.S. quarterly refunding, starting on Tuesday, is set to overshadow European and U.S. figures due later, analysts said on Friday.
But a meeting of the Group of Seven industrialised countries (G7) on Saturday is unlikely to have much impact - unless there are strong signs world leaders plan to curb the dollar strength.
"The main talking point will be the U.S. refunding next week," said David Hewitt, bond strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi International. "The feeling is that it should go fairly well."
Analysts said the UK producer price index out Monday and average earnings figures on Tuesday would also be of interest.

The U.S. Treasury surprised markets on Wednesday when it announced it will issue three, 10 and 30-year bonds worth a total of $39.75 billion dollars at the quarterly auctions, after Wall Street anticipated issues worth $37.5 billion.

The auctions, scheduled for Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, will see the issue of $17.75 billion dollars of three-year notes, $12.0 billion of 10-year notes and $10.0 billion of 30-year bonds respectively.
Analysts said they expected aggressive bidding for the new issues, after U.S. payroll data on Friday calmed worries over inflationary pressure and caused Treasuries to rally.
Hewitt said he expected Treasuries to go up rather than down after the auction, given the recent improvement in market tone.

"The traditional response is that the market backs off ahead of (an auction) then goes running after it," said Dick Howard, senior economist at Julius Baer Investments. "It's a case of nerves ahead of supply then a rally when it's absorbed."
He said recent gains could be given up on Monday and early Tuesday if the market was seen as overbought. But after that short term cap, he expected a rally out of the auctions.
"Friday's figures will certainly be positive for the supply," he said. "There's nothing there to show that inflation is going to rear its ugly head."

Opinion is mixed over whether G7 finance ministers and central banksers in Berlin will address the issue of dollar strength - a big concern for Japan. Analysts said the absence of any statement on dollar strength would move markets more than mild comments.
"If they don't say anything it would imply they're not too worried," said Howard. "If they do, it probably won't lead to any action unless it were something like, The dollar's run has gone too far'."

However, analysts said they did not expect the meeting to lead to an agreement on concerted efforts to stabilise the dollar -- although it was quite likely that there would be a verbal attempt to calm the market.

"I think whatever statement is made on exchange rates, the markets will want to test policy makers' resolve, and I think the dollar will continue to strengthen until we see actual policy moves," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ in London.
Analysts said they expected the meeting to include talks on the European single currency.

Howard said U.S. producer price figues due Friday were not generally expected to hold any surprises. Retail sales figures could be more buoyant, he said, but two together were likely to paint the now familiar picture of healthy growth but restrained inflation.
"They are significant market-moving numbers, he said, "but the markets have already factored them into prices."
The UK employment data were expected to be positive, and analysts said a slip in the average earnings forecast would boost the gilt market.
